title: The President's Face
narration_text:
Every dollar in your wallet is a death certificate with a president's face on it.

I know that sounds dramatic.
context: The narrator introduces the provocative idea that currency is linked to historical violence and death.

title: Fiat Devaluation
narration_text:
It isn't. It's actually underselling it.

The Problem: Every Fiat Currency in History Has Been Devalued To Fund Unpopular Wars.
context: The narration explains the core problem: fiat money is historically devalued to finance warfare.

title: French Revolution Start
narration_text:
Here's a fun historical pattern that definitely won't repeat itself (it will):

Revolutionary France (seventeen nineties).
context: The scene sets up the historical example of 1790s France as a recurring pattern of monetary failure.

title: The Assignats
narration_text:
Started wars with everyone.

Ran out of money.

Printed "assignats" backed by stolen church land.

Hyperinflation:
context: France's war efforts lead to the printing of land-backed currency and the onset of hyperinflation.

title: Napoleon & Weimar
narration_text:
thirteen thousand percent in five years.

Napoleon happened (not great).

Weimar Germany (nineteen twenties).
context: The narrator transitions from the fall of revolutionary France to the next historical case: Weimar Germany.

title: German Hyperinflation
narration_text:
Lost World War One.

Printed money to pay reparations.

Hyperinflation: twenty-nine thousand five hundred percent per month.
context: Post-WWI Germany attempts to pay war debts by printing money, resulting in astronomical hyperinflation.

title: Hitler's Rise
narration_text:
People burned money for heat.

Hitler happened (really not great).

United States (nineteen seventeen to present).
context: The economic collapse leads to political extremism and the transition to the United States' history.

title: The Federal Reserve
narration_text:
Created Federal Reserve (nineteen thirteen).

Immediately funded World War One (nineteen seventeen).
context: The creation of the US Federal Reserve is shown as the catalyst for funding major global conflicts.

title: Modern Devaluation
narration_text:
Dollar lost ninety-six percent of value since.

Wars now continuous and everywhere.

You're living it (how's that working out?).
context: The narrator highlights the long-term loss of the dollar's purchasing power alongside constant warfare.

title: The Money Printer
narration_text: The pattern is so consistent it's basically a law of physics: give politicians a money printer, they will use it to kill people.
context: A cynical observation that control over currency leads inevitably to military spending.

title: Trading Chickens
narration_text: Every time. Without exception. For thousands of years. You invented money to trade chickens more efficiently.
context: Contrast between the humble origins of trade and the current state of global monetary policy.

title: Incinerating Cities
narration_text:
Within a few centuries, you were using it to incinerate cities. Remarkable species.

Nineteen seventy-one: When Nixon Weaponized Money Against You.
context: A pivot to 1971, identifying it as the year the nature of money changed fundamentally.

title: Nixon's Announcement
narration_text: August fifteen, nineteen seventy-one. The day your money stopped meaning anything and nobody told you.
context: The narrator identifies a specific date as the turning point for the dollar's inherent value.

title: Ending Gold Exchange
narration_text: Nixon went on T.V. and said, in slightly more presidential language, "Remember how dollars could be exchanged for gold? We're stopping that.
context: Visualizing Nixon's famous televised address ending the gold standard.

title: New Economic Policy
narration_text:
Also, wage and price controls.
Also, import taxes." He called it a "New Economic Policy." On your planet, when someone names a policy
context: Detailing the various economic measures introduced alongside the end of gold convertibility.

title: The Naming Trick
narration_text: the opposite of what it does, something terrible is about to happen. (See also: "Patriot Act," "Affordable Care Act," "Department of Defense.").
context: A critique of political nomenclature where names often mask the true, damaging nature of policies.

title: Nixon's Motives
narration_text:
Why He Really Did It.

Vietnam War was bleeding money.

France wanted their gold back (party poopers).

Couldn't raise taxes (people riot).
context: The scene lists the pragmatic pressures—war debt and gold withdrawals—that forced Nixon's hand.

title: Economic Consequences
narration_text:
Solution: Print money forever!

What Actually Happened.

Gold standard: Dead.

Dollar backing: "Trust us bro".

Inflation: To the moon.
context: Describing the shift to fiat currency and the subsequent rapid rise in inflation.

title: The Productivity Gap
narration_text:
Your savings: Slowly murdered.

The Theft That Followed.

Since nineteen seventy-two:

Productivity up: two hundred and forty-six percent.
context: Focus on the divergence between economic productivity and individual savings since the early 70s.

title: Stolen Wealth
narration_text:
Wages up: one hundred and fifteen percent.

The difference: They stole it.

Where'd the money go? Three guesses:

Wall Street (correct!).
context: The narrator argues that the surplus value created by productivity was diverted to the financial elite.

title: The Cantillon Effect
narration_text:
War contractors (also correct!).

You (BZZT! Wrong! Thanks for playing!).

The Cantillon Effect: Why You're Poor and Raytheon Isn't.
context: Introducing the economic theory explaining why those closest to the money source benefit most.

title: Timing and Wealth
narration_text: The Cantillon Effect, understood since the seventeen hundreds: whoever gets newly printed money first gets rich. Whoever gets it last gets robbed.
context: Explaining the mechanism of the Cantillon Effect regarding the distribution of new currency.

title: Institutional Advantage
narration_text: The Fed prints money. Banks and defense contractors get it first and buy things at today's prices. By the time it trickles down to your grocery store,
context: The visual of banks and contractors spending new money before prices rise for the general public.

title: The Invisible Theft
narration_text: prices have already risen. You don't notice you've been robbed because nobody broke into your house. They just made everything in it worth less.
context: Inflation is framed as a hidden theft that devalues what people already own.

title: Misplaced Blame
narration_text: Then you blame immigrants. Which is exactly what they want you to do. (The immigrants also got robbed, by the way. You have so much in common.).
context: The narrator points out how social tension is used as a distraction from the actual source of economic hardship.

title: Medical Research Myth
narration_text:
Why "Just Fund Medical Research More" Is a Lie.

"Why not just ask for donations? Why not just increase the N.I.H. budget?
context: Transitioning to a discussion about why certain public goods are linked to military spending.

title: Money as Hallucination
narration_text:
Why tie it to military spending?".

Because money is not real. It's a shared hallucination.
context: A deep dive into the concept that money is a social construct rather than a physical reality.

title: Physics vs. Fiction
narration_text: Eight billion people pretending that the same piece of paper is worth something. Resources are real. Brains are real. Time is real.
context: Distinguishing between the fiction of currency and the tangible reality of resources and human effort.

title: Human Genius Pie
narration_text:
Money is a story you tell each other.

The Fixed Pie of Human Genius.

Eight billion brains (fixed quantity).
context: The scene introduces the idea of human potential as a finite resource that money attempts to manage.

title: Natural Limits
narration_text:
Twenty-four hours per day per brain (physics won't negotiate).

Limited raw materials (can't print titanium).
context: Listing the hard physical limits of the world that cannot be overcome by simply printing more money.

title: Finite Capacity
narration_text: Finite factory capacity (can't build infinite labs).
context: The final conclusion emphasizing that physical industrial and scientific constraints are immutable.

title: Misplaced Ingenuity
narration_text: When a brilliant engineer designs missiles, that engineer is NOT designing medical devices. When a factory builds tanks, it is NOT building M.R.I. machines.
context: The narrator illustrates the trade-off between military and medical engineering resources.

title: The One Percent Treaty Solution
narration_text: The only solution: change the ratio. Take from war. Give to life. That's what the one percent treaty does.
context: The narrator explains the fundamental purpose of the one percent treaty, which is to shift global resources away from conflict and toward the preservation of life.

title: The One Brain Limit
narration_text: When a P.h.D. researches better ways to kill people, they are NOT researching better ways to keep people alive. Every genius has exactly one brain.
context: Emphasizing that human cognitive capacity is a finite resource being diverted to defense.

title: Explosive Rentals
narration_text: You are renting forty million of them to build things that explode. This is, by a comfortable margin, the stupidest resource allocation decision
context: A critique of how modern society rents the best minds for destructive purposes.

title: Talent Distribution Reality
narration_text:
in the observable universe.

The Resource Reality.

The top ten percent of human talent is approximately eight hundred million people.
context: The narrator defines the total pool of high-level human talent available globally.

title: The Military Workforce
narration_text: Currently employed in military and defense industries: forty million (including active military, reserves, and defense contractors).
context: Stating the scale of human talent currently dedicated to defense sectors.

title: Life vs Death Ratio
narration_text:
Currently working in medical research: one million.

The spending ratio is forty point three to one for death over life.
context: A stark numerical comparison between military and medical staffing and spending.

title: Scarcity of Geniuses
narration_text: You can print infinite dollars. You cannot print geniuses. This is the most important sentence in this chapter.
context: Highlighting the fundamental difference between monetary inflation and finite human intelligence.

title: The Attention Budget
narration_text: You will forget it by tomorrow because your brain allocated its attention budget the same way your government allocates its money.
context: Explaining why critical resource allocation issues are often ignored by the public.

title: The Inflation Shell Game
narration_text:
The Inflation Shell Game (How They Steal Medical Progress).

Watch closely. This is how they rob you in broad daylight while you clap:
context: Introducing how inflation masks the lack of actual progress in medical funding.

title: Current Spending Figures
narration_text:
Today.

Global medical research is sixty-seven point five billion dollars.

Global military spending is two point seven two trillion dollars.
context: Presenting the baseline data for today's global spending priorities.

title: The Illusion of Growth
narration_text:
The ratio is forty point three to one for death.

Five Years Later (after "increasing medical research").

Medical research is up fifty percent!
context: Simulating a future scenario where medical funding seemingly increases.

title: The Monetary Mirage
narration_text:
Victory!

Military spending is also up fifty percent.

Central banks printed fifty percent more money.

Real purchasing power is exactly the same.
context: Exposing how money printing cancels out nominal budget increases.

title: Nominal Gains
narration_text:
The ratio is still forty point three to one for death.

You got a fifty percent raise. Everything costs fifty percent more.
context: Showing that even if numbers go up, the priority of death over life remains fixed.

title: A Smaller Slice
narration_text: The pie did not grow. They gave you a bigger number on a smaller slice and expected you to say thank you. You did. You always do.
context: A commentary on public acceptance of the illusion of economic growth.

title: Fifty Years of Stagnation
narration_text:
The Proof: Fifty Years of Going Nowhere.

Medical Research as percentage of G.D.P.

In nineteen seventy-five, it was zero point zero eight percent.
context: Presenting historical data showing the long-term trend of medical research funding.

title: Research GDP Share: 1985-1995
narration_text:
In nineteen eighty-five, it was zero point zero seven percent.

In nineteen ninety-five, it was zero point zero seven percent.
context: A continued data series showing the decline or plateau of research as a share of resources.

title: Research GDP Share: 2005-2015
narration_text:
In two thousand and five, it was zero point zero six percent.

In twenty fifteen, it was zero point zero six percent.
context: Showing the continued under-prioritization of research through the turn of the century.

title: The Diminishing Share
narration_text:
In twenty twenty-five, it is zero point zero six five percent.

Absolute dollars increased ten times. Share of actual resources: decreased.
context: The narrator notes that despite higher dollar amounts, the actual share of resources has shrunk.

title: Removing Smoke Detectors
narration_text:
You got richer and spent less of it on not dying. Like buying a bigger house and removing the smoke detectors.

What Actually Grew.
context: A metaphor for the dangerous trade-off between superficial wealth and survival research.

title: Growth of Other Sectors
narration_text:
The financial sector grew from three percent to eight percent of G.D.P.

The military-industrial sector grew from three percent to three point four
context: Highlighting which sectors actually expanded while medical research declined.

title: Healthcare vs Research
narration_text:
percent of G.D.P. (direct spending; broader defense-adjacent industries add more).

Healthcare spending increased from seven percent to eighteen
context: Comparing the massive rise in healthcare costs against the specific needs of research.

title: Shrinking Research Slice
narration_text:
percent of G.D.P. (most of the growth is bureaucracy, not cures).

Actual medical research is a shrinking slice.
context: Clarifying that healthcare growth is administrative, not innovative.

title: Power over Stethoscopes
narration_text: The money printers fund what they value. They value control, not cures. Nobody ever seized power with a stethoscope.
context: Explaining the political motivation behind the distribution of printed money.

title: Resources Follow the Printer
narration_text:
(Though, medically speaking, you could.).

Why Money Printing Matters: Resources Follow the Printer.
context: The narrator begins to explain the mechanics of how inflation diverts talent.

title: Defense Gets First Dibs
narration_text: When the Fed prints one trillion dollars for war, defense contractors get it first and immediately buy up the best engineers, scientists,
context: Describing how war funding allows the military to outbid other sectors for talent.

title: The Graduate's Dilemma
narration_text:
and factories.

An M.I.T. graduate with two hundred thousand dollars in student debt chooses between Raytheon at one hundred and fifty thousand
context: Using a hypothetical MIT graduate to show the financial pressure toward defense careers.

title: Postdoc vs Raytheon
narration_text: dollars or an N.I.H. postdoc at fifty-five thousand dollars. The student debt does not care about your feelings, so neither does the graduate.
context: Comparing the salary disparity between life-saving research and defense contracting.

title: Lost to the Machine
narration_text:
Another brain lost to the death machine. Multiply by forty million.

Then wonder why nobody cured your mother's cancer.
context: Linking the personal loss of loved ones to the systemic drain of scientists into the military.

title: The Deadly Ratio
narration_text: Printing more money for medicine does not work because the Fed prints even more for war, maintaining the same deadly ratio.
context: Concluding why printing money for research alone cannot fix the priority problem.

title: The Hamster Wheel
narration_text: The hamster wheel spins faster. You stay in the same place.
context: A final metaphor for the lack of real progress despite high economic activity.
